samples.summary: The load-bearing GH_MUTATION_TOKEN behaviour is never actually exercised — the stub logs argv only, not env
samples.evidence: `run()` sets `GH_MUTATION_TOKEN: "stub-app-token"` (line 102) and the STUB_GH stub records only `argv.join(" ")` into GH_STUB_LOG — it never records `process.env.GH_TOKEN`. So no test distinguishes `gh()` from `ghMutate()` (mark-ready.mjs:93-97). A regression that replaced `ghMutate(["pr","ready",...])` with plain `gh(...)` — precisely the bug the comment at mark-ready.mjs:87-92 says 'silently left gate-passing PRs stuck as drafts' — would keep every test in this file green. The only GH_MUTATION_TOKEN assertion (line 225, `assert.match(stderr, /GH_MUTATION_TOKEN/)`) merely re-asserts prose in the exit-3 error string, which is true whether or not the token is ever used.

samples.summary: --require-checks with a non-empty custom list is never pinned; the fixtures make DEFAULT_REVIEW_CHECKS and the flag indistinguishable
samples.evidence: `okConfig()` builds checkRuns from `DEFAULT_REVIEW_CHECKS` (line 72) and every promote test runs without `--require-checks`, while the only tests that pass the flag pass the EMPTY string. The real promotion path always passes the manifest-derived set (agent-review-panel.yml:1392 `--require-checks "$REQUIRED"`). A regression in the parsing at mark-ready.mjs:49-57 that ignored the flag's value and always used DEFAULT_REVIEW_CHECKS would pass all of these tests: the gate-2 failure tests use `checkRuns: []`, which fails under either required set.

samples.summary: Gate 1's discriminating logic (name === "CI" filter, latest-run-wins sort) is untested — a fail-open would stay green
samples.evidence: Every fixture uses a single workflow run named exactly "CI" (`workflowRuns: [{ name: "CI", ... }]`, line 81, and the exit-1 loop). Nothing feeds a successful run with a DIFFERENT name (which must not satisfy the gate — mark-ready.mjs:133 `filter(r => r.name === "CI")`) and nothing feeds two runs for the same SHA to pin the 'latest CI run wins' sort at mark-ready.mjs:136. Dropping either the name filter or the sort — turning an unforgeable gate into a fail-open on any successful workflow, or letting a stale successful re-run outvote a fresh failure — leaves all tests in this file passing.
searchedFor: grep for other tests referencing workflow_runs in scripts/agent

samples.summary: The label re-read fallback (`current = pr.labels` when the pre-PUT `pr view --json labels` fails) has no test and is unreachable with this stub design
samples.evidence: mark-ready.mjs:226-230 falls back to the initial snapshot when the just-before-PUT label re-read throws. The stub's `fail` matching is prefix-based on the joined argv, so `fail: ["pr view"]` also kills the FIRST read and the process exits 2 (test at line 137) — there is no way with the current stub to fail only the re-read. So the fallback branch, and the claim that the PUT is built from FRESH labels rather than the stale snapshot, are both uncovered; the 'non-agent labels survive' assertion at line 195 passes identically whether the fresh read or the stale snapshot is used, because the stub returns the same labels for both.
searchedFor: read STUB_GH fail handling in mark-ready.test.mjs

samples.summary: The exit-code inventory test only catches literal `process.exit(<digits>)`
samples.evidence: `SOURCE.matchAll(/process\.exit\((\d+)\)/g)` cannot see `process.exit(code)` or `process.exitCode = n`, so the 'no exit code outside {0,1,2,3}' guarantee is only as strong as the literal spelling; a refactor to a computed exit code would silently make the test vacuous (and `assert.ok(used.size > 0)` would then be the only thing left, which is itself near-tautological).
